To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability of blood T cells from patients and control donors to proliferative in response to human TPO or thyglobulin was not significantly different in terms of (i) lymphocyte populations tested; (ii) culture conditions; (iii) antigen source; and (iv), for the most part, the antigenic determinants tested.

T cells from patients and controls proliferated equally in response to intact TPO and TPO peptides in vitro, but T cells from some Hashimoto's thyroid patients, but not controls, responded to thyroglobulin presented by autologouos LDC.

T cell responses to thyroid autoantigens are not a universal phenomenon in patients with autoimmune thyroid disease and that T cell responses to thyroglobulin may involve the participation of B cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ability of thyroid autoantigens to stimulate T cell responses in vitro.
the identification of the antigenic determinants of human thyroid autoantigens, and the characterization of the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in their recognition by T cells.

the characterization of the thyroid autoantigens TPO and thyroglobulin, the nature of the immune response to these autoantigens, the role of T and B cells in thyroid autoimmunity, and the development of a T cell‐based immunodiagnostic assay.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are not sufficient to prove or disprove that thyroid peroxidase or thyroglobulins are T cell autoantigens in human autoimmune thyroid disease.
the T cell response to human thyroid autoantigens has not been fully characterized.

TPO/thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulins are T cell autoantigens in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves' disease, but that T cell proliferative response is not necessarily a reliable indicator of T cell autoimmunity to these thyroid antigens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the T cell responses are not as important as the B cell responses for the development of autoimmune thyroid disease.

T cell responses to thyroid peroxidise (TPO) or thyroglobin (TG) may be detected in patients with autoimmune thyroid disease (ATD) and that the presence of TPO/TG autoantibodies in the serum of patients does not necessarily indicate the presence of T cell responses.

T cells in the blood and lymphoid organs of patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves' disease do not proliferate in vitro to TPO and thyglobulin, but T cells in blood of some Hashimoto patients can proliferate to thyroglobulin presented on autologous Lymphocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

T cells from some Hashimoto's thyroid disease patients can respond to thyroid peroxidise (TPO) presented by antigen‐presenting B cells in hanging‐drop cultures, but not in conventional 200‐μi well cultures, suggesting that T cell proliferative response to TPO and thygoglobulin may be dependent on the presence of sufficient T cell precursor and appropriate antigen‐presenting cell numbers and types.
the presence of precursor T cells as well as the type and number of antigen‐present cells are critical for T‐cell responses to human T‐PO and thyroglo­bulin.
the thyroid autoantigens, TPO and thyroglubin, are capable of inducing T cell responses.
